Visualization in Python#

The folder of this notebook holds a small module, simscene, with the scenes of this course, the charts and diagrams, and what draws them. It needs NumPy and matplotlib only: every picture on this page is drawn by the notebook, not by Isaac Sim. The 3D scenes are lit the way a 3D program lights a studio shot: one lamp with soft shadows, light from the sky and from the floor, and pastel colours. Regular text in the figures is set in NVIDIA Sans, mathematics in the typeface of LaTeX, and names taken from code in Consolas; a typeface that a computer does not have is replaced by a similar one.

Show code cell source

Hide code cell source

 
# HIDE/SHOW
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from simscene import colour

colour('chapter1.ipynb')           # the code blocks of this page in the colours Notion gives them

Utilizations#

The module is built from a few small class families. Each has methods that its subclasses override, so that one call draws any member.

Base class

Scene, Chart

the same two, for boxes, arrows and text

Renderer

Renderer

Still, Canvas, Plot, Stage

draw(picture): a still picture, a 3D canvas, a Plotly figure, or prims on a USD stage

Every scene comes from one function of labs/scenes.py, the file that the lab scripts read on the DGX Spark, so this page and the simulator are given the same scene. A new scene is a subclass of LabScene with its own build; its first docstring line is its caption. A chart puts its items on a Sheet: every item has a name and values.

The code above a figure. Each folded code cell holds the script of its step, exactly as it is in labs/. It is code for Isaac Sim, so it runs on the DGX Spark and not when this page is made. The figure under it is the preview that simscene draws for that script; simscene.refresh('chapter1.ipynb') draws all of them again.

Every figure can be used, not only looked at.

What is Visualization?#

  • Visualization turns data into pictures that people can read.

  • A visualization algorithm is a transformation: data goes in, different data comes out, and at the end something can be drawn.

  • On this page each algorithm is a lab that you run inside Isaac Sim.

Types of Algorithms#

The classic algorithms fall into four families, by the kind of data they work on.

Data

Labs

Scalar

one number per sample: a height, a depth

2, 3, 4

Vector

a direction and a size per sample: a velocity

5, 6

Tensor

a \(3 \times 3\) matrix per sample: an inertia

7

Modeling

algorithms that build, sample or reduce geometry

8, 9, 10, 11

Lab 1 comes before the four families: it shows what a dataset is.

What is folded. Commands to type are always visible. Longer listings and expected outputs are folded: click a line with a triangle to open it. Above each figure, the script of its step is folded in the same way. All code is shown in the colours that Notion gives it.

What was tested, and where the pictures come from. No Isaac Sim was available while writing this course. The scripts were checked against the Isaac Sim 6.2.0.0 Python source and run against real OpenUSD with a stand-in for the simulator. That exercises the script logic and everything written to the stage, but not the physics engine, the renderer, the sensors or the stream. Three kinds of output follow from that:

  • Outputs of the NumPy-only scripts (vizcore.py, lab06a, lab08a, lab11) are quoted and real.

  • Outputs that depend only on NumPy and on what is written to the stage (Labs 1, 2, 4 and 9) are quoted as the stand-in run printed them.

  • Outputs that depend on physics, a sensor or a ray cast (Labs 3, 5, 6 B, 7, 8 B and 10) are described, not quoted. Your run supplies the numbers.

The 3D pictures on this page are previews, not Isaac Sim screenshots: each one is the scene a lab saves, drawn by the notebook from labs/scenes.py. They are lit in a studio of their own, with soft shadows and pastel colours, so their colours are softer than the colours the scripts write to the stage. Three scenes need numbers from the simulator and use stand-ins: Lab 5 (a recording made by a simple integrator), Lab 7 (the tensor from the formula) and Lab 10 (distances from the reference ray caster). The four depth pictures in Lab 3 are made from a depth image computed by a ray caster, scenes.lab03_depth(), for the same camera. The charts are computed by labs/vizcore.py, in plain NumPy, and so is everything that Play shows: the throw of Lab 5, the particles and the drops of Lab 6, and the two falls of Lab 8, which are a prediction and not a result.

Know the Four Files Every Lab Uses#

What is in it

labs/vizcore.py

The algorithms: lookup tables, marching squares, integrators, distance fields, a reference ray caster. Plain NumPy.

labs/scenes.py

What each lab shows: lab02(), lab04() and so on, each returning a list of meshes and a camera.

labs/look.py

How a scene is put on the stage: usd_scene() writes the meshes, a matte material, the camera and the light.

labs/simlab.py

The Isaac Sim boilerplate: start(), new_stage(), collide(), save(), finish().

Every lab has the same skeleton. Read it once here. start() must run before anything else from isaacsim or pxr is imported. If you change what a lab shows, change it in scenes.py.

Listing: labs/lab02_colormap.py, the skeleton of every lab 
from simlab import finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start, THEME

args = parse_args(n=65)
app = start(args.stream)

stage = new_stage()

# SOURCE and FILTER live in scenes.lab02(): a terrain, and its
# height pushed through two lookup tables.
prims, view = scenes.lab02(args.n)

# SINK: the coloured meshes go on the stage; the renderer draws.
look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)

Decide How You Will Look at Results#

Live, in the stream. Add --stream to any lab that starts the simulator. The script builds its scene, then keeps running and streams it through the scene’s camera. Connect the Isaac Sim WebRTC Streaming Client on the Mac to the Spark’s address, as in Step 4 of the page Isaac Sim on a DGX Spark. Press Ctrl-C in the terminal when you have seen enough. Only one stream can run at a time.

As a file. Every lab saves its scene as out/labNN.usda. The capture script of that Step 4 turns any of them into a picture of 1280 by 720 pixels:

# Spark (isaac)
python labs/s4_shot.py out/lab02.usda out/lab02.png

# Mac
scp spark:ivcl/courses/sim/out/lab02.png . && open lab02.png

One theme. Every lab takes --theme light (the default) or --theme dark. Use one theme for the whole session.

Lab 1: What a Dataset Is#

The idea. Any dataset has three parts. Topology says which samples are connected. Geometry says where they are. Attributes are the data they carry. Algorithms are classified by which parts they change: geometric, topological, attribute, or combined. A USD mesh stores the three parts as separate attributes, so you can watch each one change.

Show code cell source

Hide code cell source

 
# HIDE/SHOW
"""Lab 1: a dataset is topology + geometry +
attributes, and algorithms are transformations of them.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab01_dataset.py
                  python labs/lab01_dataset.py --stride 4
Output:           out/lab01.usda
"""
from simlab import finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start, THEME

args = parse_args(n=65, stride=1)
app = start(args.stream)

import os

import numpy as np
from pxr import Sdf, UsdGeom

import look
import scenes

stage = new_stage()

# SOURCE: a height field becomes a mesh prim on the stage.
prims, view = scenes.lab01(args.n, args.stride)
paths = look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)
mesh = UsdGeom.Mesh(stage.GetPrimAtPath(paths["terrain"]))


def read():
    return (np.array(mesh.GetPointsAttr().Get()),
            np.array(mesh.GetFaceVertexCountsAttr().Get()),
            np.array(mesh.GetFaceVertexIndicesAttr().Get()))


pts0, cnt0, idx0 = read()
print("--- the dataset ---")
print(f"geometry : points              {pts0.shape}")
print(f"topology : faceVertexCounts    {cnt0.shape}"
      f"  (all {cnt0[0]}-sided)")
print(f"topology : faceVertexIndices   {idx0.shape}")
print(f"first face uses points {idx0[:3]}")
print("attribute: primvars:displayColor  (one colour per point)")

# GEOMETRIC transformation: double every height.
taller, _ = scenes.lab01(args.n, args.stride, taller=True)
mesh.GetPointsAttr().Set(taller[0]["points"].tolist())
pts1, cnt1, idx1 = read()
print("--- after a geometric transformation (z * 2) ---")
print("max height   :", round(float(pts0[:, 2].max()), 3), "->",
      round(float(pts1[:, 2].max()), 3))
print("topology same:", bool(np.array_equal(idx0, idx1)
                              and np.array_equal(cnt0, cnt1)))

# ATTRIBUTE transformation: create a scalar from the geometry.
elevation = UsdGeom.PrimvarsAPI(mesh).CreatePrimvar(
    "elevation", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.FloatArray,
    UsdGeom.Tokens.vertex)
elevation.Set(pts1[:, 2].tolist())
pts2, cnt2, idx2 = read()
print("--- after an attribute transformation (elevation) ---")
print("new attribute:", elevation.GetName(),
      f"({len(elevation.Get())} values, one per point)")
print("geometry same:", bool(np.array_equal(pts1, pts2)),
      " topology same:", bool(np.array_equal(idx1, idx2)))

path = save("lab01.usda")
print(f"file size: {os.path.getsize(path) / 1024:.0f} kB"
      f" for {len(pts2)} points")
finish(app, args.stream)

What it says

In a USD mesh

Geometry

where each point is

points

Topology

which points form a face

faceVertexCounts, faceVertexIndices

Attributes

the data carried by the points

primvars:displayColor, primvars:elevation

Point at a point of the mesh to read what it carries, and at a face to see which three points make it.

In symbols. The source of this page’s terrain is a height field, two bumps and a ripple, sampled on a grid of \(n \times n\) points and shifted so that its lowest point is at height 0:

\[\begin{split} \begin{aligned} z(x, y) = {} & 0.45\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - 0.6)^2 + (y - 0.5)^2}{0.5}\right) + 0.30\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x + 0.9)^2 + (y + 0.7)^2}{0.3}\right) \\ & + 0.05\,\sin(2.5\,x)\cos(2\,y) \end{aligned} \end{split}\]

With \(n = 65\) that is \(65^2 = 4225\) points and \(2 \times 64^2 = 8192\) triangles.

Steps.

  1. Build a terrain mesh on the stage and apply two transformations to it. The last two lines of output give the saved file, out/lab01.usda, and its size.

    # Spark (isaac)
python labs/lab01_dataset.py
    Expected output 
    --- the dataset ---
geometry : points              (4225, 3)
topology : faceVertexCounts    (8192,)  (all 3-sided)
topology : faceVertexIndices   (24576,)
first face uses points [ 0 65 66]
attribute: primvars:displayColor  (one colour per point)
--- after a geometric transformation (z * 2) ---
max height   : 0.528 -> 1.056
topology same: True
--- after an attribute transformation (elevation) ---
new attribute: primvars:elevation (4225 values, one per point)
geometry same: True  topology same: True

  2. Find the three parts in the saved file. Each grep should print at least one line.

    # Spark
grep -n "point3f\[\] points" out/lab01.usda | cut -c1-80
grep -n "faceVertexIndices" out/lab01.usda | cut -c1-80
grep -n "primvars:elevation" out/lab01.usda | cut -c1-80

  3. Open labs/lab01_dataset.py and find the three comments SOURCE, GEOMETRIC transformation and ATTRIBUTE transformation. The geometric one is two lines.

    Listing: labs/lab01_dataset.py, the geometric transformation 
    # GEOMETRIC transformation: double every height.
taller, _ = scenes.lab01(args.n, args.stride, taller=True)
mesh.GetPointsAttr().Set(taller[0]["points"].tolist())

  4. Run it again keeping only every fourth sample in each direction. The points shrink from 4225 to 289.

    # Spark (isaac)
python labs/lab01_dataset.py --stride 4

  5. Look at it: run step 1 again with --stream and connect the client.

What it looks like. The scene the lab saves, out/lab01.usda:

Check yourself.

  • Doubling the heights changed the points and left both topology arrays identical. Which of the four kinds of transformation is that?

  • --stride 4 changed all three arrays. Which kind is that?

  • A lidar point cloud has geometry and attributes. What is its topology?

Lab 2: A Pipeline, and Colour Mapping#

The idea. Visualization systems are pipelines. A source creates data, filters turn data into other data, and a sink hands the result to the renderer. Colour mapping is the simplest filter: clamp a scalar to a range, normalise it, and look the result up in a table of colours. The choice of table changes what people see.

Show code cell source

Hide code cell source

 
# HIDE/SHOW
"""Lab 2: a source -> filter -> sink
pipeline that colour-maps elevation, with two lookup tables.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab02_colormap.py --stream
Output:           out/lab02.usda
"""
from simlab import finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start, THEME

args = parse_args(n=65)
app = start(args.stream)

import numpy as np

import look
import scenes
import vizcore as vc

stage = new_stage()

# SOURCE and FILTER live in scenes.lab02(): a terrain, and its
# height pushed through two lookup tables.
prims, view = scenes.lab02(args.n)

# SINK: the coloured meshes go on the stage; the renderer draws.
look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)

for p in prims:
    low = p["points"][:, 2].argmin()
    high = p["points"][:, 2].argmax()
    print(f"{p['name']:8s} colour at the lowest point"
          f" {p['colors'][low].round(2)}, at the highest"
          f" {p['colors'][high].round(2)}")
# How bright is each table from its low end to its high end?
s = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
for name, lut in (("rainbow", vc.lut_rainbow),
                  ("viridis", vc.lut_viridis)):
    lum = vc.luminance(lut(s))
    turns = int((np.diff(np.sign(np.diff(lum))) != 0).sum())
    print(f"{name:8s} brightness changes direction {turns} times")
save("lab02.usda")
finish(app, args.stream)

What it does

In this lab

Source

creates data

vc.make_terrain(): a height field of 65 by 65 samples

Filter

turns data into other data

vc.map_scalars(): a height becomes a colour

Sink

hands the result to the renderer

look.usd_scene(): meshes on the USD stage

In symbols. A value \(v\) in the range from \(v_{\min}\) to \(v_{\max}\) becomes a number \(s\) between 0 and 1 and then a colour:

\[ s = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\frac{v - v_{\min}}{v_{\max} - v_{\min}},\ 0,\ 1\right), \qquad \text{colour} = \operatorname{LUT}(s) \]

The brightness of a colour is its luminance, and in a good table it rises steadily from one end to the other:

\[ Y = 0.2126\,R + 0.7152\,G + 0.0722\,B \]

Show code cell source

Hide code cell source

 
# HIDE/SHOW

pipeline that colour-maps elevation, with two lookup tables.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab02_colormap.py --stream
Output:           out/lab02.usda
"""
from simlab import finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start, THEME

args = parse_args(n=65)
app = start(args.stream)

import numpy as np

import look
import scenes
import vizcore as vc

stage = new_stage()

# SOURCE and FILTER live in scenes.lab02(): a terrain, and its
# height pushed through two lookup tables.
prims, view = scenes.lab02(args.n)

# SINK: the coloured meshes go on the stage; the renderer draws.
look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)

for p in prims:
    low = p["points"][:, 2].argmin()
    high = p["points"][:, 2].argmax()
    print(f"{p['name']:8s} colour at the lowest point"
          f" {p['colors'][low].round(2)}, at the highest"
          f" {p['colors'][high].round(2)}")
# How bright is each table from its low end to its high end?
s = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
for name, lut in (("rainbow", vc.lut_rainbow),
                  ("viridis", vc.lut_viridis)):
    lum = vc.luminance(lut(s))
    turns = int((np.diff(np.sign(np.diff(lum))) != 0).sum())

Brightness \(Y\) from the low end to the high end

In a grey printout

Rainbow

rises and falls: it changes direction 3 times

two different heights can print as the same grey

Viridis

rises all the way

the order of the heights survives

Steps.

  1. Read the source and the filter. The scene is in labs/scenes.py, the filter is map_scalars in labs/vizcore.py.

    Listing: lab02() in labs/scenes.py, and map_scalars() in labs/vizcore.py 
    def lab02(n=65):
    X, Y, Z = vc.make_terrain(n)
    scalar = Z                                   # colour by height
    lo, hi = float(scalar.min()), float(scalar.max())
    prims = []
    for name, lut, y in (("rainbow", vc.lut_rainbow, -2.2),
                         ("viridis", vc.lut_viridis, 2.2)):
        rgb = vc.map_scalars(scalar, lo, hi, lut)
        prims.append(look.height_field(name, X, Y, Z, rgb,
                                       origin=(0.0, y, 0.0)))

    def map_scalars(values, vmin, vmax, lut=lut_viridis):
    """Clamp to [vmin, vmax], normalise, look up. Returns RGB."""
    s = (np.asarray(values, dtype=float) - vmin) / (vmax - vmin)
    return lut(s)

  2. Put the scene on the stage. The sink is one call, look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME). Then connect the client: the terrain appears twice, rainbow on the left and viridis on the right.

    # Spark (isaac)
python labs/lab02_colormap.py --stream
    Expected output

  3. Change the filter. In scenes.lab02() replace scalar = Z with the line below and run step 2 again. The terrain is now coloured by slope. This is called scalar generation: when the data has no scalar worth mapping, compute one. Put the line back afterwards.

pipeline that colour-maps elevation, with two lookup tables.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab02_colormap.py --stream
Output:           out/lab02.usda
"""
from simlab import finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start, THEME

args = parse_args(n=65)
app = start(args.stream)

import numpy as np

import look
import scenes
import vizcore as vc

stage = new_stage()

# SOURCE and FILTER live in scenes.lab02(): a terrain, and its
# height pushed through two lookup tables.
prims, view = scenes.lab02(args.n)

# SINK: the coloured meshes go on the stage; the renderer draws.
look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)

for p in prims:
    low = p["points"][:, 2].argmin()
    high = p["points"][:, 2].argmax()
    print(f"{p['name']:8s} colour at the lowest point"
          f" {p['colors'][low].round(2)}, at the highest"
          f" {p['colors'][high].round(2)}")
# How bright is each table from its low end to its high end?
s = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
for name, lut in (("rainbow", vc.lut_rainbow),
                  ("viridis", vc.lut_viridis)):
    lum = vc.luminance(lut(s))
    turns = int((np.diff(np.sign(np.diff(lum))) != 0).sum())
    print(f"{name:8s} brightness changes direction {turns} times")
save("lab02.usda")
finish(app, args.stream)

Lab 3: Colour-Map a Depth Camera#

The idea. A simulated depth camera returns one scalar per pixel: metres from the image plane. It is not a picture until you choose a range and a table. The range matters as much as the table.

In symbols. A depth \(d\) is mapped like any other scalar, with a near and a far limit as the range:

\[ s = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\frac{d - d_{\text{near}}}{d_{\text{far}} - d_{\text{near}}},\ 0,\ 1\right) \]

A fixed range uses the same limits for every frame, here 0 m and 8 m. An automatic range takes the smallest and the largest depth of the current frame.

What the depth camera looks at, the scene the lab saves as out/lab03.usda:

Show code cell source

Hide code cell source

 
# HIDE/SHOW
"""Lab 3: a simulated depth camera produces a
scalar per pixel. Capture it, then colour-map it four ways: two
tables, two ranges.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab03_depth.py
Output:           out/lab03.usda, out/depth.npy (metres, H x W),
                  out/depth_rainbow.png, out/depth_viridis.png,
                  out/depth_rainbow_auto.png,
                  out/depth_viridis_auto.png
"""
from simlab import (finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start, THEME,
                    to_np)

args = parse_args()
app = start(args.stream)

import numpy as np
import isaacsim.core.experimental.utils.app as app_utils

app_utils.enable_extension("isaacsim.sensors.experimental.rtx")
app.update()

from isaacsim.sensors.experimental.rtx import CameraSensor

import look
import scenes
import vizcore as vc

stage = new_stage()
prims, view = scenes.lab03()
look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)
save("lab03.usda")

# The depth sensor looks through the same camera as the pictures.
H, W = look.HEIGHT // 2, look.WIDTH // 2      # (height, width)
sensor = CameraSensor("/World/Camera", resolution=(H, W),
                      annotators=["distance_to_image_plane"])

app_utils.play(commit=True)
depth = None
for frame in range(120):             # the sensor needs a few frames
    app_utils.update_app()
    data, _info = sensor.get_data("distance_to_image_plane")
    if data is not None:
        depth = to_np(data).reshape(H, W)
        if frame > 10:
            break
assert depth is not None, "no depth data after 120 frames"

np.save("out/depth.npy", depth)
finite = depth[np.isfinite(depth)]
print(f"depth image {depth.shape}, {depth.dtype}")
print(f"nearest {finite.min():.2f} m, farthest {finite.max():.2f} m,"
      f" pixels with no hit: {int((~np.isfinite(depth)).sum())}")
print("wrote out/depth.npy")

# Colour mapping: two tables, each with one fixed range and with
# the range taken from this frame.
NEAR, FAR = 0.0, 8.0
lo, hi = float(finite.min()), float(finite.max())
pictures = {
    "depth_rainbow.png": vc.depth_to_rgb(depth, NEAR, FAR,
                                         vc.lut_rainbow),
    "depth_viridis.png": vc.depth_to_rgb(depth, NEAR, FAR),
    "depth_rainbow_auto.png": vc.depth_to_rgb(depth, lo, hi,
                                              vc.lut_rainbow),
    "depth_viridis_auto.png": vc.depth_to_rgb(depth, lo, hi),
}
try:
    from PIL import Image
    for name, rgb in pictures.items():
        Image.fromarray(rgb).save(f"out/{name}")
        print("wrote", f"out/{name}")
except ImportError:
    print("Pillow is not installed: no pictures written")
app_utils.stop()
finish(app, args.stream)

Lab 4: Contouring#

The idea. A contour is where a scalar field equals a chosen value. Marching squares finds it one grid cell at a time: mark each corner as above or below the value, use the pattern of four marks to pick one of 16 cases, and place the line’s crossing on each edge by linear interpolation. Two of the 16 cases are ambiguous. In 3D the same idea is marching cubes, and it is how a signed distance field becomes a collision surface.

In symbols. Four corners that are each above or below the level \(c\) give \(2^4 = 16\) cases. On an edge that the contour crosses, the crossing point is found by linear interpolation of the field values \(F_p\) and \(F_q\) at the two corners:

\[ w = \frac{c - F_p}{F_q - F_p}, \qquad \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_p + w\,(\mathbf{x}_q - \mathbf{x}_p) \]

Lab 5: Vectors, Hedgehogs and Pathlines#

The idea. A vector has a direction and a size. The most direct picture is a hedgehog: one line per sample, pointing along the vector. To see where things go over time you connect successive positions into a pathline. Colour can carry speed.

In symbols. Each cube starts with a velocity that swirls around the vertical axis and points upward:

\[ \mathbf{v}_0(x, y) = (-1.5\,y,\ \ 1.5\,x,\ \ 3)\ \text{m/s} \]

A hedgehog line runs from a position \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\mathbf{x} + k\,\mathbf{v}\) with the scale \(k = 0.08\) s, and a pathline is coloured by the speed \(\lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert\) along it.

Steps.

  1. Read how the data is recorded: one position and one velocity per body, per physics step.

    Listing: labs/lab05_vectors.py, the recording 
    t, pos, vel = [], [], []
for _ in range(STEPS):
    SimulationManager.step()
    p, _quat = bodies.get_world_poses()
    v, _omega = bodies.get_velocities()
    t.append(SimulationManager.get_simulation_time())
    pos.append(to_np(p).copy())
    vel.append(to_np(v).copy())

  2. Throw 25 cubes in a swirl and record every step.

    # Spark (isaac)
python labs/lab05_vectors.py --stream

    The script prints recorded 120 steps x 25 bodies and the range of speeds. After the run it adds two things to the scene as thin rods: one pathline per cube, coloured by speed, and a white hedgehog showing every cube’s velocity at step 30. Connect the client to see them.

  3. Make it unreadable. In scenes.lab05_overlay() change the defaults every=4 to every=1 and scale=0.08 to scale=0.5, then run step 2 again. Put the values back afterwards.

What it looks like. The scene the lab saves, out/lab05.usda. Press Play to watch the throw. The recording in this picture is a stand-in made by a simple integrator, scenes.lab05_recording(), not by Isaac Sim’s physics; yours will differ in detail, most of all after the cubes land.

# HIDE/SHOW
"""Lab 5: hedgehogs and pathlines.
Throw 25 cubes, record position and velocity at every step.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab05_vectors.py --stream
Output:           out/vectors.npz, out/lab05.usda
"""
from simlab import (collide, finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start,
                    THEME, to_np)

args = parse_args()
app = start(args.stream)

import numpy as np
import isaacsim.core.experimental.utils.app as app_utils
from isaacsim.core.experimental.prims import RigidPrim
from isaacsim.core.simulation_manager import SimulationManager

import look
import scenes

DT, STEPS, SNAPSHOT = (scenes.LAB05_DT, scenes.LAB05_STEPS,
                       scenes.LAB05_SNAPSHOT)

stage = new_stage()
prims, view = scenes.lab05_base()          # ground + 25 cubes
paths = look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)
cubes = [paths[p["name"]] for p in prims if p["name"] != "ground"]
bodies = RigidPrim(cubes)                  # the cubes move ...
collide(cubes, "convexHull")               # ... and collide
collide(paths["ground"])                   # the ground only collides

SimulationManager.set_physics_dt(DT)
app_utils.play()
app.update()

# initial velocity field: a swirl around the Z axis, plus "up"
_start, v0 = scenes.lab05_start()
bodies.set_velocities(linear_velocities=v0,
                      angular_velocities=np.zeros_like(v0))

t, pos, vel = [], [], []
for _ in range(STEPS):
    SimulationManager.step()
    p, _quat = bodies.get_world_poses()
    v, _omega = bodies.get_velocities()
    t.append(SimulationManager.get_simulation_time())
    pos.append(to_np(p).copy())
    vel.append(to_np(v).copy())
t, pos, vel = np.array(t), np.array(pos), np.array(vel)
np.savez("out/vectors.npz", t=t, pos=pos, vel=vel,
         snapshot=SNAPSHOT)
speed = np.linalg.norm(vel, axis=2)
print(f"recorded {pos.shape[0]} steps x {pos.shape[1]} bodies")
print(f"speed range {speed.min():.2f} .. {speed.max():.2f} m/s")
print("wrote out/vectors.npz")
app_utils.stop()
app.update()

# PATHLINES and HEDGEHOG: thin rods added to the scene, so they
# appear in the stream and in the saved file.
look.usd_author(stage, scenes.lab05_overlay(pos, vel, SNAPSHOT))
save("lab05.usda")
finish(app, args.stream)

Lab 6: Integration and the Time Step#

The idea. To follow a particle through a velocity field you integrate. Euler’s method steps along the current velocity; its error grows with the step. A second-order Runge-Kutta step averages the velocity at both ends and is far more accurate for the same step. A physics engine is an integrator too, and its time step plays the same role.

In symbols. For a particle at \(\mathbf{x}_k\) in a velocity field \(\mathbf{v}\) and a step \(\Delta t\) the two methods are

\[\begin{split} \begin{aligned} \text{Euler:} \quad & \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k + \Delta t\,\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}_k) \\ \text{Runge-Kutta 2:} \quad & \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k + \frac{\Delta t}{2}\,\Bigl(\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}_k) + \mathbf{v}\bigl(\mathbf{x}_k + \Delta t\,\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}_k)\bigr)\Bigr) \end{aligned} \end{split}\]

Part A uses the field \(\mathbf{v}(x, y) = (-y,\ x)\) whose exact paths are circles.

"""Lab 6, part B: a physics engine is a numerical
integrator. Drop the same cube with three different time steps
and compare each run with the exact free-fall curve.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab06b_timestep.py
Output:           out/timestep_240.csv, _60.csv, _15.csv
"""
from simlab import (collide, finish, new_stage, parse_args, start,
                    THEME, to_np)

args = parse_args()
app = start(args.stream)

import numpy as np
import isaacsim.core.experimental.utils.app as app_utils
from isaacsim.core.experimental.prims import RigidPrim
from isaacsim.core.simulation_manager import SimulationManager

import look
import scenes

Z0, SIZE, DURATION = (scenes.LAB06_Z0, scenes.LAB06_SIZE,
                      scenes.LAB06_DURATION)
table = []
for hz in scenes.LAB06_RATES:
    stage = new_stage()
    prims, view = scenes.lab06()           # ground + cube at 2 m
    paths = look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)

    collide(paths["cube"], "convexHull")
    collide(paths["ground"])

    SimulationManager.set_physics_dt(1.0 / hz)   # before play
    app_utils.play()
    app.update()

    rows = []
    for _ in range(int(DURATION * hz)):
        SimulationManager.step()
        p, _quat = body.get_world_poses()
        rows.append((SimulationManager.get_simulation_time(),
                     float(to_np(p)[0, 2])))
    rows = np.array(rows)
    rows[:, 0] -= rows[0, 0] - 1.0 / hz   # first sample is t = dt
    np.savetxt(f"out/timestep_{hz}.csv", rows, delimiter=",",
               header="t,z", comments="")
    table.append((hz, np.diff(rows[:, 0]).mean(),
                  scenes.lab06_error(rows), rows[:, 1].min(),
                  rows[-1, 1]))
    app_utils.stop()
    app.update()

exact = np.sqrt(2 * (Z0 - SIZE / 2) / 9.81)
print(f"exact impact time {exact:.4f} s; rest height {SIZE / 2} m")
print("  Hz   mean dt    error at t=0.4 s   lowest z   final z")
for hz, dt, error, lowest, final in table:
    print(f" {hz:4d}  {dt:.5f}    {error:+.4f} m"
          f"          {lowest:.4f} m   {final:.4f} m")
finish(app, args.stream)

  2. Read the two methods. They differ by one line.

    Listing: integrate() in labs/vizcore.py 
    def integrate(velocity, x0, dt, steps, method="euler"):
    """Follow a particle through a velocity field.

    velocity(x) -> v. method is "euler" or "rk2".
    Returns positions of shape (steps + 1, dim).
    """
    x = np.asarray(x0, dtype=float)
    path = [x.copy()]
    for _ in range(steps):
        v = velocity(x)
        if method == "euler":
            x = x + dt * v
        elif method == "rk2":
            x = x + dt / 2 * (v + velocity(x + dt * v))
        else:
            raise ValueError(method)
        path.append(x.copy())
    return np.array(path)

The algebra behind the gap (open it after you have answered)

A loop that updates the velocity first and the position second has, after \(k\) steps, the velocity \(v_k = -g\,k\,\Delta t\) and the height

\[ z_k = z_0 - g\,\Delta t^2 \sum_{i=1}^{k} i = z_0 - \tfrac{1}{2}\,g\,t^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}\,g\,t\,\Delta t, \qquad t = k\,\Delta t \]

The first two terms are the formula. The third is the gap: the loop is below the formula by \(\tfrac{1}{2}\,g\,t\,\Delta t\) and that is proportional to the time step. This is what first order means. At \(t = 0.4\) s it is 3.27 cm for 60 steps per second, the middle row of the table under the chart.

Lab 7: Tensors, the Inertia of a Rigid Body#

The idea. A \(3 \times 3\) symmetric tensor describes a quantity that differs with direction. Its eigenvectors are three perpendicular principal axes; its eigenvalues are the sizes along them. It is drawn as an ellipsoid or as three axes. Every rigid body in a simulator carries such a tensor: its inertia.

In symbols. A solid box with mass \(m\) and edge lengths \(a \times b \times c\) along its own axes has the inertia tensor

\[\begin{split} \mathbf{I} = \frac{m}{12} \begin{bmatrix} b^2 + c^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & a^2 + c^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & a^2 + b^2 \end{bmatrix} \end{split}\]

Its principal axes \(\mathbf{e}_i\) and principal moments \(\lambda_i\) solve the eigenvalue problem

\[ \mathbf{I}\,\mathbf{e}_i = \lambda_i\,\mathbf{e}_i, \qquad i = 1, 2, 3 \]

Steps.

  1. Predict. The box is 0.6 by 0.5 by 0.2 m and weighs 2 kg. For a box, the moment about an axis is \(\tfrac{m}{12}\) times the sum of the squares of the two other edges. Compute the three moments by hand. Which axis has the largest?

  2. Read the tensor from the physics engine.

    # Spark (isaac)
python labs/lab07_inertia.py --stream

    The script prints the mass, the tensor the engine reports, the formula’s tensor, the principal moments and axes, and then the tensor again after turning the box 30 degrees about Z. It adds the three principal axes to the scene as rods above the box, red, green and blue, with length proportional to the moment.

  3. Read the two calls that matter.

# HIDE/SHOW
"""Lab 7: the inertia of a rigid body is a tensor.
Read it from the physics engine and find its principal axes.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab07_inertia.py --stream
Output:           out/inertia.npz, out/lab07.usda
"""
from simlab import (collide, finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start,
                    THEME, to_np)

args = parse_args()
app = start(args.stream)

import numpy as np
import isaacsim.core.experimental.utils.app as app_utils
from isaacsim.core.experimental.prims import RigidPrim

import look
import scenes
import vizcore as vc

stage = new_stage()
prims, view = scenes.lab07_base()            # ground + box

body = RigidPrim(paths["box"], masses=[scenes.LAB07_MASS])

collide(paths["ground"])

app_utils.play()
app.update()


def read_tensor():
    return to_np(body.get_inertias()).reshape(3, 3)


mass = float(to_np(body.get_masses()).ravel()[0])
measured = read_tensor()
expected = vc.box_inertia(mass, *scenes.LAB07_EDGES)
vals, vecs = vc.principal_axes(measured)

print("inertia tensor from the engine (kg m^2):\n", measured)
print("formula m/12 (b^2+c^2, a^2+c^2, a^2+b^2):\n", expected)
print("principal moments:", vals)
print("principal axes (columns):\n", vecs)

# Turn the box 30 degrees about Z and read the tensor again.
half = np.radians(30) / 2
body.set_world_poses(orientations=[np.cos(half), 0, 0, np.sin(half)])
app.update()
turned = read_tensor()
print("after a 30 degree turn about Z:\n", turned)
print("same numbers as before:", bool(np.allclose(measured, turned,
                                                   atol=1e-5)))
np.savez("out/inertia.npz", tensor=measured, turned=turned, mass=mass)
print("wrote out/inertia.npz")
app_utils.stop()
app.update()

# The principal axes, as three rods above the box.
look.usd_author(stage, scenes.lab07_axes(measured))
save("lab07.usda")
finish(app, args.stream)

Lab 8: Implicit Functions and Collision Shapes#

The idea. An implicit function \(F(x, y, z)\) describes a shape by an equation. It is negative inside, zero on the surface and positive outside, and shapes combine with min and max. When \(F\) is the distance to the surface, contours at small positive values are offset surfaces: free safety margins. Physics engines use exactly these ideas for collision, and the collision shape you choose is a model of the mesh, not the mesh.

In symbols. A shape is the set of points where its function is negative:

\[ F(\mathbf{x}) < 0 \ \ \text{inside}, \qquad F(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \ \ \text{on the surface}, \qquad F(\mathbf{x}) > 0 \ \ \text{outside} \]

A circle with centre \(\mathbf{c}\) and radius \(r\) is \(F(\mathbf{x}) = \lVert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c} \rVert - r\) and two shapes \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) combine as

\[ \text{union: } \min(F_1, F_2), \qquad \text{intersection: } \max(F_1, F_2), \qquad \text{difference: } \max(F_1, -F_2) \]

for level, name in ((0.0, "surface"), (0.1, "10 cm offset")):

      f"(F = {part[60, 60]:+.2f})")

    def demo_part(xs):
    """A part built from three distance functions on the grid
    xs x xs: a disc, minus a hole, minus a slot."""
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, xs, indexing="ij")
    disc = sdf_circle(X, Y, (0.0, 0.0), 1.0)
    hole = sdf_circle(X, Y, (0.0, 0.0), 0.5)
    slot = sdf_box(X, Y, (0.9, 0.0), (0.5, 0.15))
    ring = op_difference(disc, hole)             # disc minus hole
    return op_difference(ring, slot)             # ... minus a slot

from simlab import (collide, finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start,
                    THEME, to_np)

args = parse_args()
app = start(args.stream)

import isaacsim.core.experimental.utils.app as app_utils
from isaacsim.core.experimental.prims import RigidPrim
from isaacsim.core.simulation_manager import SimulationManager

import look
import scenes

DT = 1 / 120
rows = []
for approximation in ("convexHull", "convexDecomposition", "sdf",
                      "none"):
    stage = new_stage()
    prims, view = scenes.lab08()             # ground, ring, ball
    paths = look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)

             else "through the hole")

    app_utils.stop()
    app.update()

with open("out/colliders.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write("approximation,ball_z\n")
    f.writelines(f"{a},{z:.4f}\n" for a, z in rows)
print("on the ground the ball centre would be at",
      scenes.LAB08_BALL_R, "m")

Lab 9: Glyphs#

The idea. A glyph is an object whose position, direction, size or colour is driven by data. A hedgehog line is the simplest glyph. USD draws thousands of copies of one prototype cheaply with a point instancer: one cone, many positions, orientations and scales.

In symbols. At a sample with unit surface normal \(\mathbf{n}\) the cone’s own axis is turned onto the normal, and its length \(\ell\) grows with the slope \(1 - n_z\) of the terrain:

\[ \ell = 0.12\,\bigl(1 + 6\,(1 - n_z)\bigr)\ \text{m} \]

Steps.

  1. Read the instancer: one prototype and three per-glyph arrays.

    Listing: labs/lab09_glyphs.py, the point instancer 
    # ONE cone is stored; the instancer draws it once per sample.
glyphs = UsdGeom.PointInstancer.Define(stage, "/World/Glyphs")
cone = look.mesh("cone", *look.cone_shape(scenes.LAB09_RADIUS),
                 look.WHITE_RGB, lit=False)
matte = UsdShade.Material.Get(stage, "/World/Look/Matte")
proto = look.usd_mesh(stage, "/World/Glyphs/Proto", cone, matte)
glyphs.CreatePrototypesRel().AddTarget(proto.GetPath())
glyphs.CreateProtoIndicesAttr([0] * len(bases))
glyphs.CreatePositionsAttr(bases.tolist())
glyphs.CreateOrientationsAttr(
    [Gf.Quath(*map(float, q)) for q in quats])
glyphs.CreateScalesAttr([(1.0, 1.0, float(s)) for s in lengths])

"""Lab 9: glyphs. One cone per sample, turned

Output:           out/lab09.usda

import scenes

steep = lengths.argmax()

      f" cone length {lengths[steep]:.3f} m")

Lab 10: Probing#

The idea. Probing samples one dataset at the points of another. Every simulated sensor is a probe: a camera probes the scene with a grid of rays, a lidar with a fan. Sample too sparsely and thin things vanish between samples.

In symbols. A fan of \(n\) rays spread over an angle \(\Theta\) leaves a gap \(\Delta\theta\) between neighbouring rays, and an object of width \(w\) at a distance \(d\) covers an angle of about \(\alpha\) radians:

\[ \Delta\theta = \frac{\Theta}{n - 1}, \qquad \alpha \approx \frac{w}{d} \]

The fan is certain to hit the object only when \(\Delta\theta \le \alpha\) holds.

Show code cell source

Hide code cell source

 
# HIDE/SHOW
"""Lab 10: probing. A sensor samples the scene
along rays; how many rays decides what the robot can see.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab10_probe.py --stream
Output:           out/probe.npz, out/lab10.usda
"""
from simlab import (collide, finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start,
                    THEME)

args = parse_args()
app = start(args.stream)

import numpy as np
import isaacsim.core.experimental.utils.app as app_utils
import omni.physics.core
from isaacsim.core.simulation_manager import SimulationManager

import look
import scenes
import vizcore as vc

stage = new_stage()
prims, view = scenes.lab10_base()            # ground + obstacles
paths = look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)
collide([paths[p["name"]] for p in prims if p["name"] != "ground"])

app_utils.play()
app.update()
SimulationManager.step()

query = omni.physics.core.get_physics_scene_query_interface()
measured = {}
for n, _rgb, _width, _lift in scenes.LAB10_FANS:
    directions = vc.ray_fan(n, scenes.LAB10_FOV)
    dist = np.full(n, np.inf)
    for i, d in enumerate(directions):
        ok, hit = query.raycast_closest(
            scenes.LAB10_ORIGIN, tuple(map(float, d)),
            scenes.LAB10_MAX, True)
        if ok:
            dist[i] = hit.distance
    measured[n] = dist
    reference = scenes.lab10_reference(n)
    both = np.isfinite(dist) & np.isfinite(reference)
    worst = np.abs(dist[both] - reference[both]).max() \
        if both.any() else float("nan")
    leg = vc.raycast_boxes_2d(scenes.LAB10_ORIGIN, directions,
                              scenes.LAB10_BOXES[2:])
    print(f"{n:3d} rays: {int(np.isfinite(dist).sum()):3d} hits,"
          f" thin leg seen by {int(np.isfinite(leg).sum())} rays,"
          f" max difference to reference {worst:.4f} m")

np.savez("out/probe.npz", **{f"dist_{n}": d
                             for n, d in measured.items()})
print("wrote out/probe.npz")
app_utils.stop()
app.update()

# The rays, as rods from the sensor to what each one hit.
look.usd_author(stage, scenes.lab10_rays(measured))
save("lab10.usda")
finish(app, args.stream)

    dist = np.full(n, np.inf)

  2. Probe two boxes and a thin leg with a fan of 10 rays and a fan of 90 rays, both 60 degrees wide.

python labs/lab10_probe.py --stream

    For each fan the script prints the number of hits, how many rays the thin leg should catch, and the largest difference between the engine’s distances and the reference ray caster. The script adds the rays to the scene as rods: red for the fan of 10, green for the fan of 90.

  3. Find the threshold. In scenes.py change the 10 in LAB10_FANS to 30, then 45, then 60, and run step 2 each time.

Check yourself.

  • Do the engine’s distances agree with the reference? What is the largest difference?

  • The leg is 6 cm wide and 4.5 m away. What angle does it cover? What ray spacing guarantees a hit?

  • What is the smallest number of rays in a 60 degree fan that always sees it?

  • More rays cost compute. Name one other way to avoid missing the leg.

Lab 11: Data Reduction#

The idea. Data grows faster than the ability to draw or simulate it, so you reduce it first and accept an error. Subsampling keeps every n-th sample of regular data. Decimation does the equivalent for arbitrary meshes. The question is always how much error each step of reduction costs.

In symbols. Keeping one sample in every \(k\) along both axes turns a grid of \(n \times n\) points into one with \((n - 1)/k + 1\) points on a side. The error is measured after rebuilding the full grid \(\hat{z}\) from the reduced one by linear interpolation:

\[ e_{\max} = \max_i\,\lvert z_i - \hat{z}_i \rvert, \qquad e_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (z_i - \hat{z}_i)^2} \]

Hide code cell source

 
# HIDE/SHOW
"""Lab 11: data reduction by subsampling. How
much error does each level of reduction cost? Plain NumPy; the
simulator is not started.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab11_reduction.py
"""
import vizcore as vc

print("stride  points   quads   max error   rms error")
for stride, points, quads, worst, rms, _Xs, _Zs in vc.reduction_table():
    print(f"{stride:5d}  {points:6d}  {quads:6d}"
          f"   {worst:.4f} m   {rms:.4f} m")

# HIDE/SHOW
"""Lab 1: a dataset is topology + geometry +
attributes, and algorithms are transformations of them.

Run (env isaac):  python labs/lab01_dataset.py
                  python labs/lab01_dataset.py --stride 4
Output:           out/lab01.usda
"""
from simlab import finish, new_stage, parse_args, save, start, THEME

args = parse_args(n=65, stride=1)
app = start(args.stream)

import os

import numpy as np
from pxr import Sdf, UsdGeom

import look
import scenes

stage = new_stage()

# SOURCE: a height field becomes a mesh prim on the stage.
prims, view = scenes.lab01(args.n, args.stride)
paths = look.usd_scene(stage, prims, view, THEME)
mesh = UsdGeom.Mesh(stage.GetPrimAtPath(paths["terrain"]))


def read():
    return (np.array(mesh.GetPointsAttr().Get()),
            np.array(mesh.GetFaceVertexCountsAttr().Get()),
            np.array(mesh.GetFaceVertexIndicesAttr().Get()))


pts0, cnt0, idx0 = read()
print("--- the dataset ---")
print(f"geometry : points              {pts0.shape}")
print(f"topology : faceVertexCounts    {cnt0.shape}"
      f"  (all {cnt0[0]}-sided)")
print(f"topology : faceVertexIndices   {idx0.shape}")
print(f"first face uses points {idx0[:3]}")
print("attribute: primvars:displayColor  (one colour per point)")

# GEOMETRIC transformation: double every height.
taller, _ = scenes.lab01(args.n, args.stride, taller=True)
mesh.GetPointsAttr().Set(taller[0]["points"].tolist())
pts1, cnt1, idx1 = read()
print("--- after a geometric transformation (z * 2) ---")
print("max height   :", round(float(pts0[:, 2].max()), 3), "->",
      round(float(pts1[:, 2].max()), 3))
print("topology same:", bool(np.array_equal(idx0, idx1)
                              and np.array_equal(cnt0, cnt1)))

# ATTRIBUTE transformation: create a scalar from the geometry.
elevation = UsdGeom.PrimvarsAPI(mesh).CreatePrimvar(
    "elevation", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.FloatArray,
    UsdGeom.Tokens.vertex)
elevation.Set(pts1[:, 2].tolist())
pts2, cnt2, idx2 = read()
print("--- after an attribute transformation (elevation) ---")
print("new attribute:", elevation.GetName(),
      f"({len(elevation.Get())} values, one per point)")
print("geometry same:", bool(np.array_equal(pts1, pts2)),
      " topology same:", bool(np.array_equal(idx1, idx2)))

path = save("lab01.usda")
print(f"file size: {os.path.getsize(path) / 1024:.0f} kB"
      f" for {len(pts2)} points")
finish(app, args.stream)

Check yourself.

  • What is the largest stride that keeps the error under 1 cm? By what factor did the point count fall?

  • Each doubling of the stride divides the points by four. By roughly what factor does the maximum error grow?

If Something Fails#

What to do

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'isaacsim'

The environment is not active. Run conda activate isaac.

A lab stops at an isaacsim import or call

The scripts use the isaacsim.core.experimental modules of Isaac Sim 6.2. Check pip show isaacsim. Almost all simulator calls are in labs/simlab.py; what a lab draws goes through plain USD in labs/look.py. A version difference will show up in simlab.py or in the few isaacsim imports at the top of a lab.

Nothing appears in the streaming client

Only one stream can run at a time, and it must be a script started with --stream. See Troubleshooting on the page Isaac Sim on a DGX Spark.

A body falls through the ground or an obstacle

It has no collider. Every lab calls collide(...) for the things that should collide, the ground included; check that line.

no depth data after 120 frames in Lab 3

The renderer was still loading. Run the lab again; the second start is faster.

Your capture is too bright, too dark or too contrasty

See the end of Step 4 on the page Isaac Sim on a DGX Spark: DOME_INTENSITY in labs/look.py, and the renderer’s tone mapping.
